We do a lot of really good work in reducing single occupancy vehicles on the roadway. And so Sam's going to talk a little bit about how we may even be able to do a little bit more.

So with that, I'll turn it over to Sam. Great. Thank you so much. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for having me. My name is Sam Chanisman. I am the Proffered Transportation Demand Management Coordinator for FCDOT. And just as a quick recap for those that might not be as familiar, uh tdm is all about reducing congestion on our roads so removing single occupancy vehicles through a set of strategies whether that's getting people on transit carpool telework other active transportation methods and we have a whole team that works a lot on promoting the resources that the county has um which i believe you guys heard from marcus more team lead a few

weeks ago with the best workplaces for commuters and the resources that we give to them my work is a little bit more specific to developments in the county that have a legal proffered obligation to do TDM as they proffered to our TDM guidelines through their entitlement processes. And so let me get to the next slide here. So these guidelines were adopted in 2013 and essentially established a reduction goal expectation for different office and residential uses that come through the entitlement process. And the way that that works is when they come in for an application using the

International Transportation Engineer's Handbook, we can estimate the amount of trips a site is projected to bring onto our network. And then based on a certain amount of rates, which I'll go into a little bit more later, those developments are expected to prove to us that they're reducing that projected amount by a certain percentage. So generally, what do these guidelines outline for a TDM program? They're first and foremost designed to be flexible. So prior to 2013 guidelines, We had a lot of very specific TDM proffers that had, you know, very specific standards,

like you have to have a shuttle between X and Y hour, and it's just very constraining. And the best TDM programs are designed to be flexible, ones that are able to adapt with the times. Like a few years ago, we had a lot of shift to telework, and programs under these guidelines were able to adjust accordingly and able to have very site-specific strategies that work best for them.

And so what these guidelines also outline is a TDM plan that they submit to us that we kind of review to make sure, you know, these are the strategies that they want to do for the site, and we approve those, and then if they need to change it, they're able to submit amendments to those without having to go through the full entitlement process again.

Additionally, these guidelines set out to set up a TDM account to make sure that these developments are having money set aside for these strategies in the plan and work plan, a remedy fund, which is an account that the development sets up in the case that these goals somehow aren't being met.

And so we have a fallback then that they can draw upon in the case that somehow the TM accounts depleted and the strategies that we had approved previously hadn't worked. And it also serves as an incentive for developments in Tyson specifically as they, for those developments that exceed their goals, they can earn back that money in the remedy fund that they've set aside.

Additionally, another Tyson-specific one is we have a penalty fund, and this is if everything goes awry and all these fallbacks have gone astray. The county can draw upon a cash escrow or a letter of credit to go in and implement strategies ourselves should the remedy fund strategies not work as well.

And we've never had to implement that one before, which I think is a great marker of success for our program. Additionally, the guidelines set out methodologies for traffic counts and surveys. These are how we monitor and make sure that these programs are meeting their goals.

They do a study to show that they're under the threshold of allowable trips. And then the surveys also allow us to see how employees or residents are using the program and how the TDM plan or work plan can shift overall.

So a little bit more about the reduction rates that we have today. As I said, they were established in 2013. The county commissioned a study which determined a base rate of reduction for the county with the kinds of transit we have available to begin with, you know, metro, bus.

And then using that base rate determined a trip reduction goal based on your distance to metro. So in this example map here, I've got the West Falls Church metro. And so if you're falling in that orange circle closest to metro, you're within a quarter mile from the station. And if you were in office, we'd expect your trip reduction goal to be between 35 and 45 percent.

um the range kind of is um determined based on a conversation with an applicant um you know if you're further out from metro and maybe don't have as much bus connectivity we might have you closer to the lower end of threshold versus the higher and vice versa and then the guidelines also set out specific guidelines for tyson's um as it's a more designated urban dense area with a lot of development. And so this chart I know is a little more confusing, but essentially the way it works is the more development that there is in Tyson's, the higher expectation there is for TDM for these

developments. So right now we're still under this first category of up to 65 million gross square feet of development. But as you can see, the rates are a little bit higher because if you're on Metro's doorstep, you've got a little bit of built-in TDM with that as well. So with all that said, as kind of a recap of our guidelines as they stand today.

What's changing and why? So the guidelines have been in place for a little bit over a decade now with not much change at all. And so based on feedback from industry and the data that we've been seeing these developments report as they've been required to annually, we're proposing a few updates to our guidelines and how they work.

So I had kind of mentioned the Remedy Fund release previously. That's that incentive mechanism in Tyson's that allows developments that exceed their goal to earn back money that they've set aside in their remedy fund by proving to us that, you know, they've got a robust TDM program that exceeds the goal that they've proffered to, and we want to reward that for not just in Tyson's, but all areas of the county.

So the first thing that we want to do is open up that release mechanism for more than just Tyson's developments. The second thing is updated language regarding TDM funding and operating accounts. A lot of the feedback that we receive from developments is we have all these different accounts that they have to set up separately with interest-bearing funds.

And so this would allow them to streamline it into one account with line items but continue to report to us the various expenditures that they have for TDM annually and make it a little bit more streamlined for them in how they operate these TDM programs.

Additionally, a streamlined process for TDM plan submission. I'd kind of mentioned a TDM plan and work plan separately. This was established in the guidelines and is a bit redundant, so we're merging the two into just one plan submission, which would make it easier for both staff and for developments as well.

Additionally, we're updating language surrounding transportation management associations, specifically with the sunsetting of the Tyson's partnership and just the lack of TMAs in other areas. We are having to be more of an optional part of our guidelines, or at least one that's a little bit more flexible in how it's written without specifically naming a TMA by name, but rather joining a TMA generally.

As a result of all this, the sample proffers that we have for developers will be cleaner than the ones from above. And additionally, we want to add in a building-by-building option for TDM. Another big thing that we've heard from the programs that we have in place today is that when these developments come in site-wide, there's one building that will come online a lot earlier than the others and has to bear the brunt of the TDM program for the rest of the buildings, and that includes cost and setting up marketing.

And so this way is just a little bit more equitable for different owners that come in first and that the other ones later also pull their weight in this TDM program we can monitor accordingly. And then this next slide, we've got updated resources for developers.

Again, the guidelines were created a decade ago, so we've got a few broken links in that document that needs some updating for sure. And then finally, most notably, which I'll delve into next, is an update to our reduction rates. So I spent some time explaining those, and what we're seeing currently is that developments are really exceeding these goals and blowing them out of the water across the county.

And we just want to make sure that the guidelines that we have in place today are right-sized to what we're seeing out and observing in the real world. And that way we can have more accurate traffic studies when they come into rezoning or other entitlement processes and making sure that we're right-sizing those applications as well and not overbuilding or providing the correct amount of other resources as well.
